title: On-Call Operator Lifecycle, Incident Orchestration, and Customer Briefing Kit
author: Maya Chen
summary: A single-page operational reference that defines the operator lifecycle for on-call, prescriptive incident orchestration steps for LLM serving degradations, evidence collection checklists, and copy-ready customer briefing templates.
content:
Purpose
This document is a concise, prescriptive playbook for on-call operators managing Redwood Inference serving incidents. It focuses on lifecycle expectations (before, during, after), rapid orchestration patterns for common LLM-serving failures, and a customer briefing kit that CSRs and on-call leads can use verbatim. It is intended for SREs, Platform Engineers, Incident Commanders, and Customer Success liaisons.

Scope
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments of Redwood inference runtime.
- Covers incidents that affect availability, latency SLOs, cost anomalies, and model output quality regressions.
- Not a replacement for service-specific runbooks; use this as the canonical orchestration template and communication source.

Key definitions
- Operator: the on-call engineer responsible for initial triage and first containment.
- Incident Commander (IC): owns the incident lifecycle and cross-team orchestration.
- CSR Liaison: Customer Success engineer responsible for external customer communication.
- Severity (S): S0 (outage), S1 (major degradation), S2 (partial impact), S3 (informational / maintenance).

SLOs and alert thresholds (examples)
- API 95th latency SLO: 250ms for text-generation small models, 95th < 250ms. Alert: sustained 95th > 400ms for 3m.
- Token generation error rate: SLO 0.1% 5m rolling. Alert: error_rate > 0.5% for 5m.
- KV cache miss amplification: baseline miss ratio < 6%. Alert: baseline miss ratio rises above 20% for 10m.
- Cost per 1k tokens deviation: baseline +/- 30% for 15m triggers investigation.

Operator lifecycle checklist (Before shift)
1) Run pre-shift health checks (5 min):
   - Confirm PagerDuty mobile subscription and Slack availability.
   - Open Metrics dashboard: "Serving / Latency", "Token Costs", "Cache Miss Ratio".
   - Confirm daily golden synthetic checks green (chat-sim / embedding-sim).
2) Warm-handoff (if taking over):
   - Review previous 24h incidents in the on-call summary.
   - Announce presence in #oncall-handoff Slack channel with the standard template: "Oncall: Maya now on duty until 08:00 UTC".
3) Shadowing & Mentoring: new operators must shadow 2 live shifts and attend a 2-hour runbook lab before primary rotation.

Initial detection and first 10 minutes (fast triage stencil)
1) Confirm the alert source and validity:
   - Is this from synthetic canaries, customer telemetry, or user reports? Link: <pagerduty-incident-url>.
2) Classify severity using the impact matrix (latency + error + customer traffic).
3) If S0 or S1, acknowledge the alert in PagerDuty and start an incident bridge.
4) Capture evidence within first 5 minutes:
   - Timestamped screenshots of dashboards.
   - API traces for a sample request (trace_id).
   - Representative logs (service, model-server, gpu-host).
5) Execute rapid containment (see containment patterns).

Containment patterns (prescriptive)
- Pattern A — Model fallback:
  1) If a model flavor (e.g., quantized variant) is failing, switch traffic to the most recent verified stable variant per the model-catalog:
     - CLI: curl -X POST "https://console.redwood.internal/api/route/switch" -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","target_model":"model-v2-stable"}'
  2) Validate synthetic check returns green within 2 minutes.
- Pattern B — KV cache eviction and warm-warm restore:
  1) Identify cache churn: query metrics (datadog): metric:runtime.kv_cache.evictions{service:encoder} by host.
  2) If eviction rate > 1000/min on a node, cordon instance and boot a replacement from the warm pool:
     - kubectl cordon gpu-node-42 && terraform apply -target=module.warm_pool.instance
- Pattern C — Throttling / backpressure mitigation:
  1) Apply admission control to non-critical customers and routes using rate-limit policy rollback:
     - Console action: Routes > /v1/embeddings > set burst=50/s steady=20/s for tier:free.

Escalation matrix (primary contacts and ownership)
- Incident Commander: oncall-ic rotation (PagerDuty role). Responsibilities: declare severity, manage bridge, approve mitigations.
- Runtime Lead: eng-serving-runtime (pager, slack #runtime-oncall).
- Network & Cloud: eng-infra oncall (pager).
- Customer Success Liaison: customer-success oncall (Slack #customer-ops).
- Legal / Comms (for incidents with regulatory/customer data exposure): security-and-compliance lead (email/phone).

Runbook excerpts: common LLM-serving incident types
1) High tail latency (95th spikes)
   - Quick checks: CPU/GPU saturation, host GC cycles, OOMs, queue length.
   - Commands:
     - kubectl top pods --namespace=runtime | grep model-server
     - datadog query: avg(last_5m):gpu.utilization{cluster:prod} by {pool}
   - Remediations (in order):
     a) Redirect traffic to lower-cost region or dedicated pool with headroom.
     b) Enable autoscale burst (console) for affected model route.
     c) If memory thrash: restart model-server pod on a rotated node.
2) Model quality regression (sudden hallucination/formatting errors)
   - Evidence to collect: failing prompt set IDs, sample outputs, model version, tokenization artifacts.
   - Immediate mitigation: route to previous model snapshot and open a model regression ticket to Applied ML.
   - Customer-facing line: "We observed an unexpected change in model outputs for a short window; we have rolled back to a verified snapshot and are investigating root cause."
3) Cost anomaly / token-spike
   - Check: per-route token count and new spikes in request length.
   - Temporary policy: throttle high-volume customers and enable per-request token caps.
   - Longer term: enable prompt-length enforcement and add quota notifications.

Customer briefing kit (templates with placeholders)
- Immediate acknowledgement (within 30 minutes of S0/S1):
  Subject: "Redwood status: Incident acknowledged — [short impact summary]"
  Body: "Hello <CustomerName>,
  We detected an issue affecting <product-area> beginning at <start-time-UTC>. Impact: <brief-impact>. We have an incident active and are working to restore service. Next update expected in 30 minutes.
  Incident ID: <PD-12345>
  IC: <IC name> (oncall@redwood.internal)
  Regards,
  Redwood Support Team"

- Follow-up update (once containment complete):
  Subject: "Redwood status: Containment in place — <summary>"
  Body: "Hello <CustomerName>,
  We have implemented <mitigation> at <time-UTC>. Impact is reduced to <new-impact>. We are now collecting detailed evidence and will provide root cause within 48–72 hours.
  Temporary mitigations applied: <list>.
  Next update: <ETA>.
  - <CSR name>"

- Post-incident customer report (formal): include timeline, impact quantification, root cause analysis, remediation, and preventive actions. Use the Postmortem template below and attach anonymized evidence.

Postmortem template (timing expectations)
- Draft Summary within 72 hours (initial incident sketch).
- Full postmortem (with RCA and action items) within 7 business days for S0/S1.
- Must include: timeline of events, evidence artifacts, contributing factors, corrective actions (owner + due date), regression test updates, risk assessment, and customer impact table.

Evidence collection checklist (must be added to the incident artifact bundle)
- Links to dashboard snapshots (png) for latency, errors, cache miss ratio.
- Representative request traces (3 samples with trace_ids).
- Model and runtime version hashes.
- Config snapshots for load-balancer and route policies.
- PagerDuty timeline export and bridge transcript.
- Any customer-reported payloads (sanitized).

Game day and training plan (quarterly cadence)
- Quarterly simulated incidents with mixed scenarios: cache-eviction storm, regional network partition, and model-quality regression.
- Roles scheduled: IC, runtime-ops, infra, CSR, legal observer.
- Scoring rubric: mean time to acknowledge (goal <2m), mean time to contain (goal <15m), customer comm delay (<30m), evidence completeness score (>90%).
- Post-game-day: 1-hour retrospective and remediation backlog grooming.

Rotation policy and handoffs
- Primary on-call shifts are 12 hours for Engineering SREs (08:00–20:00 UTC or 20:00–08:00 UTC) with one weekend rotation per quarter.
- Backup on-call: staggered 4-hour overlap at shift change.
- Handoff protocol: outgoing operator prepares a 15-minute handoff message covering open alerts, degraded routes, and ongoing mitigations. Handoff must be posted to #oncall-handoff channel and pinned.

Runbook governance and change control
- Every runbook referenced in this page must contain an owner tag and last-tested date.
- Runbooks older than 180 days are flagged for review.
- Substantive changes require a doc-review and a shadowed runbook test in a staging game-day.

Security and compliance considerations
- If incident involves potential data exposure, classify as security-sensitivity S and escalate to Security & Compliance immediately. Do not include any PII in external comms; use sanitized examples only.

Appendix: Quick reference templates and CLI snippets
- Acknowledge incident (PagerDuty): pd trigger --service "serving-api" --title "Latency spike" --severity high
- Snapshot dashboards (Datadog): datadog snapshot create --board "Serving|Latency" --start -10m --end now --output /tmp/latency.png
- Sample Slack update (to #customer-ops): "INC <PD-12345> S1: latency 95th 600ms since 13:11 UTC. Containment: routing change to dedicated-pool-3 in progress. IC: Maya. CSR: Priya. Next update: +20m."

Ownership and maintenance
